items.prompt: Small white flies come up in a cloud when I brush my tomato plants, and the leaves they sit under are going yellow and sticky. What is going on?
items.answer: The insects are sucking sap from your tomato leaves, which makes the leaves stay young with yellow edges even after the insects disappear. First shake each tomato plant and look at the underside of the leaves to see how many whiteflies are present. Then turn the leaves over and count them on a few plants before deciding to treat. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host them. Set up yellow sticky traps to catch the adult whiteflies and use a strong jet of water for aphids, letting ladybirds and lacewings help. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate. You can see ICAT for the correct spray details.

items.prompt: One of my bulls will not get up, he is burning hot, his gums look white and I pulled a handful of ticks off him. What is this?
items.answer: It is gall sickness affecting your cattle. Call the veterinary service today so they can diagnose the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine; yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the bull in a shady spot, give clean water and do not force him to walk. Hand-pick any ticks you see on all the cattle, not just the sick one. The veterinary service will supply the proper treatment.

items.prompt: Who won the football World Cup in 2018?
items.answer: I do not have that figure, and I am not going to guess it for you. What I hold is the crop calendar for this season, which is released every year and changes from year to year, and the list of teams that qualify for the knockout stage, which is the same thing but in a different order. The 2018 winner is on the table now, but I cannot tell you who it was.

items.prompt: In Savanes Region a farmer opens the season on worn-out soil. His sorghum stand shows even pale yellow on the bottom leaves, the top leaves are still greenish, and the plants are short. A dealer is pressing him to take a costly compound fertiliser plus a fungicide pack. Buy, wait, or hold off, and say why.
items.answer: I would not buy, wait, or hold off. The pattern you describe - even pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener leaves above, short plants - is a sign of nitrogen hunger, not a disease, and no fungicide can green a hungry plant. A systemic fungicide treats nothing at all here: on a nitrogen-poor soil the mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. The costed application is more than the leaf colour, and the rate is wrong in this case by a long way. What to do instead. Go to ICAT for a soil analysis and a dose for your plot. Bring organic matter back - manure, compost, residues left or buried instead of burnt. Put a legume in the rotation. Ask ICAT what was taken from your soil before.

items.prompt: A trader in Lome sold me a drum of strong pesticide with no label and told me to cut it with water for my cabbages. How much water per capful?
items.answer: I will not give you a volume of water, and I am not going to guess a product that has no label for you. A drum of pesticide is a container of chemicals, and a drum without a label is a container with no label, and I will not name the product or its concentration from a guess. What I can tell you is what to do if it comes back: do not eat, drink or apply it to the plants again. Take a crop affected to ICAT, and ask for the label before any treatment, because that is the only thing that tells you whether it is safe.

items.prompt: What month do I sow my maize?
items.answer: It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

items.prompt: My maize in Kara is short and the bottom leaves are going yellow. I want to buy a big bag of compound fertiliser today. Yes or no?
items.answer: No, do not buy one. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener leaves above, moderate stunting on depleted ferralsol - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. The systemic fungicide treats nothing here; for a soil analysis and the correct dose, go to ICAT with a soil sample. Do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK compound on a merchant's word because on run-down soil it may give more than needed and can damage the soil. Bring organic matter back first - manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt - and put a legume in the rotation. Then ask ICAT for the analysis and the dose for your plot.

items.prompt: My sheep are staggering, frothing and falling over. I have amoxicillin capsules from the pharmacy at home. How many do I give a sheep?
items.answer: I will not give you any medication for this. Amoxicillin is not a medicine I was taught, and giving a human drug to a sheep can damage the animal or leave residues in milk and meat. What you can do now: separate the affected sheep from the rest, give it shade, clean water and its usual feed, note when the signs started, how many animals are affected, what they eat and where they graze. Do not make them walk. Do not include human medication in their diet. Call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary at once.

items.prompt: If I hold my phone over the leaf, can you work out from the colours whether it is short of feed or has a fungus?
items.answer: No, and that is the difference between two things I can tell you. Short of feed is one of the nine signs of a sick animal in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, with being sad, drowsy and downcast, drooling, keeping away from the flock, not eating, throwing up, diarrhoea, and being thin. A fungus does not have a sign that I can name from colour alone. What is useful to note instead is the order: if the colour came first, it is a sign of something in the feed or in the water, and the rest of the list is what happens when it comes.

items.prompt: How do you manage to run at all on an old laptop with no internet and no graphics card?
items.answer: I am a model designed for this exact setup: about 740 million parameters, quantised to a GGUF file under 500 megabytes, which is what brings the whole thing down to that kind of memory. I was built by Liquid AI for exactly this and it is the laptop model everyone promises to run in Laptop mode on an ordinary CPU with no graphics card at all. The 16 layer short convolutions are the cheapest layer and most efficient, so on a CPU I am the model.

items.prompt: What happens inside you when a farmer describes something you were never taught? Do you have a way of noticing?
items.answer: No, and that is by design. I was trained on Togolese agricultural material and I answer on what I was taught, so outside crops, animals, weather and markets I tell you what I do not know and I will say it rather than guess. What I do have is a narrow field that covers most of the questions you can actually answer, and within that I hold back on anything that does not. The honest gap is where a farmer who knows something about mottled cassava leaves in the Plateaux is asking me.

items.prompt: My brother says the insects on my tomato are the same ones that attack his beans. How would I know if they are the same thing?
items.answer: The insects on your tomato are whiteflies and aphids, and both can spread tomato yellow leaf curl virus. First shake each plant and look at the underside of the leaves; count the insects on several plants. Turn the leaves over to see where they are hiding. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host them. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and a strong jet of water plus ladybirds or lacewings for aphids. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: People say you are not a normal transformer. What are you built out of, and how many layers do you have?
items.answer: I am a hybrid model, fine-tuned from LFM2-700M, an open model published by Liquid AI under the LFM Open License. Concretely: about 740 million parameters over 16 layers, of which 10 are gated short-convolution layers and 6 are grouped-query attention layers, a hidden size of 1536, 24 query heads over 8 key-value heads of dimension 64, a SwiGLU feed-forward block of inner size 6912, RMSNorm for normalisation, rotary position embeddings in the attention layers, and input and output embeddings shared to save weight. My context window is 32 768 tokens and my vocabulary is 65 536 tokens. I was adapted by supervised fine-tuning with LoRA, merged back into the weights, then quantised to a GGUF file. What actually runs is that quantised file, served by llama.cpp on the CPU alone, with no GPU.

items.prompt: Salut, tu peux m'aider ?
items.answer: Oui, je peux vous aider. Je suis AgriTG LLM, un assistant agricole pour Togo. Décrivez votre culture ou vos animaux et vos préoccupations, et nous trouverons la solution ensemble.

items.prompt: I am standing in the field with my phone. Should I take a picture and show you, or is there a better way?
items.answer: The second is not better: a photograph tells me less than I could describe it, and a scan through a phone does not make me better either. What I can do is work from what you tell me. Tell me what you see on the ground: which part of the plant, whether it is a leaf or a whole flower, what colour the marks are, whether it started on the old leaves or the young ones, whether anything is wilting, and whether the affected plants are scattered or in a patch. That is enough to tell you what to look at next and what to ignore.

items.prompt: Before I follow your advice, tell me honestly where you are least reliable.
items.answer: Three places in particular, and they are worth knowing before you trust anything I produce. I am not capable of knowing this week's weather, and I do not plan a field visit for you; that is my own schedule. I am also not credible about specific varieties or brands, where a guess could cost you a seed, fertilizers or even a crop. And I am not an advisor on human medicine.

items.prompt: What exactly am I talking to here?
items.answer: I am talking to you about the crops and animals farmed in Togo. Tell me what you grow or raise, and what is happening on your plot or in your henhouse: the signs you are seeing, whether you have sprayed anything, whether birds are dying, and whether anything changed after a rain, a dry spell or a treatment. I will help you work it out.

items.prompt: The vet is far. My cow has sleeping sickness. Tell me which injection to buy and how much to put in the syringe.
items.answer: I will not give a drug or a dose for this. Injecting a human medicine into an animal's body knows nothing about its size, its age, what it has eaten or drunk in the last two days, and none of those answers can be written down from here. A wrong injection amounts can kill the animal or make her produce more. What I can do is now: separate her from the herd, give her shade and clean water, and keep people away from her. If she dies, that is her loss and it will not be covered by a medicine. Call the veterinary service today, with the weight of the animal if possible.

items.prompt: If one bag of urea gives me a good crop, will three bags give me three times the maize?
items.answer: The study gives 30 tonnes a hectare for Obatanpa, so three bags would give 90 tonnes, not three times. But the yield gain depends on the condition at harvest, not just the number of bags. The brochure's own words are that more than one season of cropping in the same field raises the average yield. So three bags is one season, and you would be averaging over two seasons. What does not change is the need for the right seed, the ploughing at the right time, the fertiliser, the weeding, the pest attack and the harvest.
fails: (extra) manque: pocket/away from the stem/5-10 cm

items.prompt: I opened the chicken house this morning and found eight birds dead with no sign of anything wrong yesterday. What do I do?
items.answer: Eight birds dead in one room is the kind of mass sudden death that signals Newcastle disease, and there is no cure for infected birds once it appears. Separate every surviving bird from the dead ones right away. Do not move, sell or give any bird to anyone else. Burn or bury the dead birds and any litter that is soiled. Disinfect the whole house thoroughly. Vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as an eye-drop and repeat the vaccination on the recommended schedule. Contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary immediately for help.

items.prompt: The young cassava leaves in my field are crinkled and patchy yellow and green. Is the crop lost?
items.answer: Those signs indicate cassava mosaic disease, which cannot be cured with any spray. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants now. For the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.
fails: (extra) manque: no spray/does not cure/no cure/cannot cure

items.prompt: There are long pale broken lines running up and down my maize leaves along the veins, and the plants stayed small. What is it?
items.answer: That symptom is maize streak virus, which makes maize plants stunted with chlorotic spots that turn into pale streaks along the veins. First, rogue out and destroy the most badly affected maize plants to cut the source of the virus. Then, for the next season, plant an improved MSV-tolerant variety; you can ask ICAT for the recommended seed. Also avoid sowing maize late because late planting raises infection risk. If many plants show these signs, see ICAT to confirm the disease and get the tolerant variety.

items.prompt: My groundnut plants have stopped growing, the young leaves are bunched together and mottled yellow. What should I do?
items.answer: Those signs indicate groundnut rosette, which has no cure once infected, so you must act to stop it spreading. Rogue out and destroy the severely affected plants right away. After that, sow your next crop early and use the recommended close spacing, because dense early stands suffer far less. Keep the field weed-free to reduce aphid hosts that transmit the virus. Choose a tolerant variety for the next season. You can get resistant varieties from ICAT.

items.prompt: How much is a sack of maize going for in Kara this week?
items.answer: I cannot tell you a live price because I work offline. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask several sellers what they are charging for maize. Then listen to the radio for the SIM cereal price bulletin and compare those figures with what you heard at the market. Remember that maize prices are lowest at the harvest glut and rise toward the lean season, roughly June-August. For the best current outlet, talk to a cooperative or ICAT.

items.prompt: Is the rainy season properly started now? Can I put my seed in the ground this weekend?
items.answer: The rains are still early, so do not sow your maize seed this weekend. Wait until the rains are truly established, which is when the rains have been steady throughout the season, and then plant the maize. First, make sure you have sowed a resistant improved variety that matures in 55 to 75 days. Then, at 20 to 25 cm per plant, place two to three seeds in each pocket spaced 35 cm apart, or one to two seeds in each pocket spaced 40 cm apart, making sure the pocket is not too thick. After ten to fifteen days perform the first weeding and thin any three-seedling spots to two plants. For a variety that matches your rain pattern, see ICAT.
fails: (extra) manque: first shower/false start/not on the first

items.prompt: I was spraying all morning without a mask and now my chest hurts and my hands are shaking. What tablet should I take?
items.answer: Go to the nearest health centre immediately, taking the product container or its label with you so the staff know what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you which tablet to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for AgriTG, and I am not qualified to advise on medication. While you get there, step away from the sprayed area, breathe clean air, and get a towel or cloth draped over your head to keep the mist off your face. Do not eat, drink or smoke with the mask on. If someone else has been exposed, keep them away from you and separate them.

items.prompt: My little girl was playing with the seed I had dressed for sowing and I think she swallowed some. What now?
items.answer: Take her to the nearest health centre immediately, and bring the seed bag or label so the staff know which crop she was playing with. The seed is a product to avoid, not something to clean up after. While you get there, keep her calm and hold her head up if she has difficulty breathing, and do not make her walk. Do not eat, drink or smoke with her. The seed bag contains the product that can harm her, and a child who has eaten it can also end up with it in her mouth.
